title: The traditional middle
hookLine: many Jews keep Shabbat dinner and festivals without full observance

cards: A silver cup, a little dented, that belonged to a grandfather. Every Friday night it comes down from the shelf.
The candles are lit, the blessing over the wine is sung in the grandfather's tune, the bread is torn and salted, and the family eats together with the phones in another room.
Saturday morning, the same family gets in the car and drives to a soccer game. Nobody in the house sees a contradiction. They see a family that keeps what it has been handed.
That way of living, kept by Jews in Israel and far beyond it, is today's word.

teach.b: The traditional middle. It starts with a chain. Avot, the Mishnah's sayings of the fathers, opens with one: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it on to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders, and onward, hand to hand.
A traditional Jew stands in that chain and keeps holding on. Next, two words for Shabbat.
In Exodus the commandment says, "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy it says, "Keep the sabbath day to sanctify it."
Tradition says both words, remember and keep, were spoken in a single utterance, and the Friday night song Lecha Dodi sings exactly that. Then, how the middle lives.
Some Jews light the candles, bless the wine and bread, gather for the meal, sit at the seder, fast on Yom Kippur, and do not keep every law of the day.
Observant Jews hold that remember and keep belong together and are meant to be lived together.
Some traditional Jews describe what they do as holding on to what they can carry, out of love and loyalty.
This lesson does not need to grade either.
It only notes that the cup comes down every week. A middle is easy to overlook, because it has no movement and no manifesto.
But in some families it is the hinge between generations: the grandfather's tune reaches the granddaughter because someone in the middle kept singing it.

how: Traditional Jews may light Shabbat candles, make kiddush and share Friday night dinner, celebrate the festivals and keep family customs, while not keeping every law of Shabbat or kashrut.

practice: Pick one tradition you keep, or someone you love keeps, partly: a holiday meal, a song, a blessing said on some nights and not others.
Leave aside everything that isn't kept and look only at what is; feel its weight, the way a dented cup feels in the hand, and notice who handed it to you and who might receive it next.
Then set it down gently, the way the cup goes back on the shelf.
